clinicalPearls: A fulminant, multi-organ variant of antiphospholipid syndrome causing widespread small-vessel thrombosis over days, in contrast to the single large-vessel events typical of classic APS
Suspect in any patient with known or suspected antiphospholipid antibodies who develops rapidly progressive multi-organ dysfunction
Roughly half of cases are precipitated by an identifiable trigger such as infection, surgery, trauma, anticoagulation withdrawal, or malignancy
Renal, pulmonary, cerebral, cardiac, cutaneous, and adrenal involvement are the most commonly affected sites
Thrombocytopenia and schistocytes may be present, creating overlap with thrombotic microangiopathy syndromes and complicating diagnosis
Mortality remains high despite treatment, so early recognition and aggressive combination therapy are critical
A definite diagnosis requires histopathologic confirmation of small-vessel occlusion in at least one organ, though treatment should not be delayed pending biopsy in critically ill patients
harrison.pathophysiology: Catastrophic APS represents an accelerated, disseminated form of antiphospholipid antibody-mediated thrombosis affecting predominantly small vessels and multiple organs simultaneously, rather than the single medium/large-vessel thrombi seen in classic APS. Antiphospholipid antibodies (anticardiolipin, anti-beta2-glycoprotein I, lupus anticoagulant) activate endothelium, platelets, and complement, driving a systemic thrombo-inflammatory cascade that resembles disseminated intravascular coagulation but with predominant thrombosis rather than bleeding. A triggering event (infection, surgery, trauma, or abrupt anticoagulant discontinuation) is thought to initiate a self-amplifying cytokine storm and complement activation, leading to a vicious cycle of endothelial injury and microthrombosis across organs. This results in a systemic inflammatory response with multi-organ failure occurring within days to weeks.
additionalDifferentials: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura / atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome
Disseminated intravascular coagulation (from sepsis or malignancy)
Thrombotic microangiopathy secondary to malignancy or drugs
infectionMimics: Severe sepsis / septic shock with multi-organ failure and coagulopathy
Disseminated intravascular coagulation triggered by systemic infection
additionalInvestigations: Antiphospholipid antibody panel (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-beta2-glycoprotein I) — confirms underlying antibody-driven process
Complete blood count with peripheral smear — detects thrombocytopenia and schistocytes suggesting microangiopathic hemolysis
Coagulation studies (PT, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer) — assesses for overlapping consumptive coagulopathy
Renal and liver function panels — screens for organ involvement and severity
ADAMTS13 activity — helps exclude thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura as an alternative or coexisting diagnosis
Imaging (CT/MRI) of suspected organs — identifies infarcts in brain, lung, kidney, or bowel
Tissue biopsy of an accessible affected organ (skin, kidney) — provides histologic confirmation of small-vessel thrombosis when feasible
Blood and other relevant cultures — evaluates for an infectious trigger or mimicking sepsis
redFlags: Rapid development of dysfunction in three or more organ systems within days
New thrombocytopenia with schistocytes in a patient with known antiphospholipid antibodies
Recent surgery, infection, or anticoagulant interruption in a patient with lupus or prior thrombosis
Adrenal hemorrhage/infarction presenting as unexplained hypotension or adrenal insufficiency
Concurrent cardiac (valvulopathy, myocardial infarction) and pulmonary (ARDS) involvement
Rapid clinical deterioration despite therapeutic anticoagulation
pitfalls: Mistaking catastrophic APS for straightforward sepsis-related multi-organ failure or DIC and delaying antibody testing
Withholding anticoagulation and immunosuppression while awaiting confirmatory biopsy in a rapidly deteriorating patient
Failing to identify and treat the precipitating trigger (e.g., untreated infection) alongside the antibody-driven process
Overlooking coexisting thrombotic microangiopathy, which may require additional therapies beyond standard APS management
harrison.prognosis: Catastrophic APS carries a high mortality rate even with aggressive combination treatment, though survival has improved with earlier recognition and multimodal therapy. Survivors remain at risk for recurrent thrombotic events and organ damage, requiring long-term anticoagulation and monitoring.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Antiphospholipid Syndrome chapter (Rheumatologic and Immunologic Disorders section)
